title: Scientists recreated a bird song recorded in the 1960s using a computer; modern sparrows began copying it
source_used: The Guardian, 13 Oct 2026 (Times of India page returned no text)
key_facts: Scientists made a computer-generated version of a rufous-collared sparrow song last heard in a Buenos Aires park in the 1960s, rebuilt from hand-drawn annotations.
Less than three months later a local bird began to copy parts of the song.
Gabriel Mindlin, professor of physics at the University of Buenos Aires, co-authored the study.
The song is still sung by a few individuals close to where it was played.
Researchers hope synthetic recordings could help tutor birds of species whose populations are dwindling.
The Guardian says AI could help provide live tutoring in the future (a possibility, not a result).
quote_evidence: Less than three months later, a local avian resident began to copy parts of the song.
It is possible that AI could help provide live tutoring in the future.
why_it_matters_hint: Computer-made songs might help rebuild lost bird culture in declining species.
event_date: Study date not stated; Guardian article 13 Oct 2026
notes: Times of India page gave no text; read The Guardian's longer piece on the same study. The Guardian text mentions AI only as a future possibility, so the AI angle is slight.
